steps.observation: You have 900 seconds. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Here’s a high‐level, step-by-step picture of how a Transformer works conceptually. Think of it as replacing recurrent or convolutional sequence models with layers of “attention” that can look anywhere in the input in parallel.

1.   Input Representation  
     •  Token embedding: each input token (word, subword, etc.) is mapped to a d-dimensional vector.  
     •  Positional encoding: since there’s no recurrence, we add (or concatenate) a position-dependent signal so the model knows the order of tokens.

2.   The Attention Mechanism (the core idea)  
     •  For each position, we compute three vectors—Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V)—by projecting the token embedding through learned linear transforms.  
     •  Attention scores: we take dot-products of the Query at position i with all Keys in the sequence, scale by √d, and apply softmax. That gives a distribution over positions.  
     •  Weighted sum: we multiply those softmax weights by the corresponding Values and sum them up. The result is a context-aware representation for position i.

3.   Multi-Head Attention  
     •  Instead of doing one big attention, we split Q/K/V into h subspaces (“heads”), each of lower dimension.  
     •  We run attention in parallel on each head, letting each focus on different types of relationships (e.g. syntax, coreference, long-range).  
     •  Finally we concatenate all the head outputs and linearly project back to the original dimension.

4.   Position-wise Feed-Forward  
     •  After multi-head attention, each position’s vector goes through the same small two-layer feed-forward network (with a nonlinearity in between).  
     •  This lets the model mix up and re-scale the information at each position independently.

5.   Residual Connections + Layer Normalization  
     •  Around each sub-layer (multi-head attention and feed-forward) we add the input (“residual”) to the output, then apply layer norm.  
     •  This stabilizes training and lets gradients flow more freely.

6.   Stacking into an Encoder (and Decoder)  
     Encoder: you stack N identical layers, each with  
       a) multi-head self-attention (every token attends to every other)  
       b) feed-forward  
     Decoder (for sequence generation/translation): also N layers, but each layer has three sub-layers:  
       a) masked self-attention (prevent attending to future output tokens)  
       b) encoder–decoder attention (allow each output position to attend to all encoder positions)  
       c) feed-forward

7.   Generating or Classifying  
     •  At the top of the decoder you project the final vectors into the vocabulary space and apply softmax to get next-token probabilities.  
     •  For tasks like classification, you might just pool or take the “first” token’s vector and feed it to a classifier layer.

8.   Training  
     •  Typically trained with teacher forcing and cross-entropy loss on next-token (or target-token) prediction.  
     •  All weights—including Q/K/V projections, feed-forward weights, positional-encoding parameters—are learned end-to-end by backprop.

9.   Why Transformers Shine  
     •  Parallelism: the entire sequence is processed at once, so training can fully utilize GPUs/TPUs.  
     •  Flexibility: self-attention can link distant tokens directly, capturing long-range dependencies more easily than RNNs.  
     •  Scalability: models like BERT (encoder-only), GPT (decoder-only) or full encoder-decoder (e.g. T5) are all straightforward variants.

In short, a Transformer is a stack of layers that repeatedly let every position “attend” to every other position (via QKV dot-product attention), then mix that information with simple feed-forward networks, all tied together by residual connections and layer norms. This modular, highly parallel design is what powers today’s state-of-the-art NLP models.
